name: The example
why: 13: exchange 12 for 6, 4 and 3, then sell all three, because none of them is worth exchanging. 6 + 4 + 3 = 13 is more than 12.

name: Zero
why: 0: a coin with 0 on it is worth nothing.

name: Selling is better
why: 11: exchanging gives 5 + 3 + 2 = 10, so sell the coin.

name: Twice
why: 27: 24 becomes 12, 8 and 6. Exchange the 12 again (13 rupees) and sell 8 and 6: 13 + 8 + 6 = 27.

name: Every n below 40
why: Every small case, one after another. If your memo is a global dict, it must still give the right answers when the function is called many times.

name: One million
why: 2,566,393. Plain recursion asks for the same amounts again and again and makes millions of calls here; a memo works out each amount once, a few hundred amounts in all.

name: One billion
why: Plain recursion makes billions of calls here. With a memo, only a few hundred different values are ever reached (n divided by products of 2, 3 and 4), so it is instant.

name: 10¹²
why: A table with one entry for every amount up to n would need a million million entries. Memoisation stores only the values the recursion reaches: this is where top-down beats a table.

name: 10¹⁸
why: Still only a few thousand different values, and about 60 calls deep (each call at least halves n).
